subject: computing pi (and volume of a hypersphere) with Stan using Monte Carlo integration

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: computing pi (and volume of a hypersphere) with Stan using Monte Carlo integration
parts:
Here's a Stan program I wrote for the Machine Learning
Summer School in Sydney next week to illustrate how
Monte Carlo integration can be used to compute the
mathematical constant pi. This is THE textbook example
of Monte Carlo.

/**
* Compute the mathematical constant pi by Monte Carlo integration.
*
* First, sample (x,y) uniformly from a square with vertices (-1,1),
* (-1,1), (1,-1), (1,1) by sampling x and y independently from the
* interval (-1,1).
*
* Second, determine if (x,y) lies within the circle circumscribed in
* the square, by testing if (x^2 + y^2 < 1). Then multiply the
* proportion of points inside the circle by the area of the square (4 here)
* to produce a Monte Carlo estimate of the area of the circle.
*
* A circle with radius r has area pi * r^2, so setting r=1, yields
* an area of pi.
*
* NOTE: Run with fixed parameter algorithm and zero warmup iterations.
*/
model {
}
generated quantities {
real<lower=-1,upper=1> x;
real<lower=-1,upper=1> y;
real<lower=0,upper=4> pi;
x <- uniform_rng(-1,1);
y <- uniform_rng(-1,1);
pi <- 4 * (x^2 + y^2 < 1);
}

You could actually eliminate x and y by defining

pi <- 4 * (uniform_rng(-1,1)^2 + uniform_rng(-1,1)^2 < 1);

but I left them in because I thought it'd be useful to be able
to plot the draws (for instance, with one color inside the circle
and another outside).


Here's how I called it in RStan:

> fit <- stan("pi.stan", algorithm="Fixed_param",iter=1e4,warmup=0)

and here's the fit:

> print(fit)
Inference for Stan model: pi.
4 chains, each with iter=10000; warmup=0; thin=1;
post-warmup draws per chain=10000, total post-warmup draws=40000.

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
x 0.00 0.00 0.58 -0.95 -0.5 0 0.5 0.95 40000 1
y 0.00 0.00 0.58 -0.95 -0.5 0 0.5 0.95 39364 1
pi 3.14 0.01 1.64 0.00 4.0 4 4.0 4.00 40000 1


I wouldn't enter any digit competitions for pi with MC integration,
because the error only goes down at a rate of O(1/sqrt(M)) where M is the
number of MC draws, so each decimal place requires on the order of
100 times more samples. The nice thing about pure Monte Carlo (as
opposed to Markov chain Monte Carlo) is that each draw is independent,
so n_eff should be equal to the sample size (it won't be exactly that
because of the approximate nature of the n_eff calc, which doesn't
know MC was in play).

- Bob

P.S. Here's a more general program to compute the volume of
a hypersphere:

/**
* Compute the volume of a hypersphere of a given radius in a
* given number of dimensions by Monte Carlo integration.
*
* The volume will be the mean of the sampled sphere_volume values.
*/
data {
int<lower=1> N;
real<lower=0> radius;
}
transformed data {
real cube_volume;
cube_volume <- (2 * radius)^N;
}
model {
}
generated quantities {
vector<lower=-1, upper=1>[N] x;
real<lower=0,upper=cube_volume> sphere_volume;

for (n in 1:N)
x[n] <- uniform_rng(-1,1);

sphere_volume <- cube_volume * (dot_self(x) < radius);
}

If you feed it data (N=2, radius=1), you get the same result as
the simpler program in the main body of this e-mail.

I probably won't have time to do the more general case in class.

P.P.S. This is totally going in the manual :-)

I also just realized this is a model for which the median
is a terrible summary, because all the draws of pi are
either 0 or 4. So medians aren't going to work well for
any discrete distribution, like a Bernoulli, because you'll
get 0 or 1 (or maybe 1/2 if you have the same number of
0s and 1s and you interpolate).

- Bob

That’s awesome. I love that line of output:
pi 3.14 …

When explaining this one, it perhaps would be helpful to emphasize that this is a somewhat atypical example in that the inference of interest is for the expectation of a binary predictive quantity, rather than a parameter or function of parameters.

But, hey, this is making me think: we could simulate Buffon’s needle! Although this is a bit tricky because if we’re using it to compute pi, we wouldn’t want to “cheat” by drawing signs and cosines. I guess we could draw from a bivariate normal and then normalize the vector . . . still seems a bit complicated, though.

>>>
>>>
>>> Here's how I called it in RStan:
>>>
>>>> fit <- stan("pi.stan", algorithm="Fixed_param",iter=1e4,warmup=0)
>>>
>>> and here's the fit:
>>>
>>>> print(fit)

>>> 4 chains, each with iter=10000; warmup=0; thin=1;
>>> post-warmup draws per chain=10000, total post-warmup draws=40000.
>>>
>>> mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
>>> x 0.00 0.00 0.58 -0.95 -0.5 0 0.5 0.95 40000 1
>>> y 0.00 0.00 0.58 -0.95 -0.5 0 0.5 0.95 39364 1
>>> pi 3.14 0.01 1.64 0.00 4.0 4 4.0 4.00 40000 1

>>> I wouldn't enter any digit competitions for pi with MC integration,
>>> because the error only goes down at a rate of O(1/sqrt(M)) where M is the
>>> number of MC draws, so each decimal place requires on the order of

>>> opposed to Markov chain Monte Carlo) is that each draw is independent,

Yes, good point. I’d only been thinking about inference for parameters (which in Stan are necessarily continuous) but I hadn’t been thinking about predictive quantities.

>>>>
>>>> Here's a Stan program I wrote for the Machine Learning
>>>> Summer School in Sydney next week to illustrate how
>>>> Monte Carlo integration can be used to compute the
>>>> mathematical constant pi. This is THE textbook example
>>>> of Monte Carlo.
>>>>
>>>> /**
>>>> * Compute the mathematical constant pi by Monte Carlo integration.
>>>> *
>>>> * First, sample (x,y) uniformly from a square with vertices (-1,1),
>>>> * (-1,1), (1,-1), (1,1) by sampling x and y independently from the
>>>> * interval (-1,1).
>>>> *
>>>> * Second, determine if (x,y) lies within the circle circumscribed in
>>>> * the square, by testing if (x^2 + y^2 < 1). Then multiply the
>>>> * proportion of points inside the circle by the area of the square (4 here)
>>>> * to produce a Monte Carlo estimate of the area of the circle.
>>>> *
>>>> * A circle with radius r has area pi * r^2, so setting r=1, yields
>>>> * an area of pi.
>>>> *
>>>> * NOTE: Run with fixed parameter algorithm and zero warmup iterations.
>>>> */
>>>> model {
>>>> }
>>>> generated quantities {
>>>> real<lower=-1,upper=1> x;
>>>> real<lower=-1,upper=1> y;
>>>> real<lower=0,upper=4> pi;
>>>> x <- uniform_rng(-1,1);
>>>> y <- uniform_rng(-1,1);
>>>> pi <- 4 * (x^2 + y^2 < 1);
>>>> }
>>>>
>>>> You could actually eliminate x and y by defining
>>>>
>>>> pi <- 4 * (uniform_rng(-1,1)^2 + uniform_rng(-1,1)^2 < 1);
>>>>
>>>> but I left them in because I thought it'd be useful to be able
>>>> to plot the draws (for instance, with one color inside the circle
>>>> and another outside).
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> Here's how I called it in RStan:
